title: Quantum Relaxometry Under Continuous Wave Excitation
authors: Vladimir Verkhovlyuk, Chayma Bouchair, Oleg A. Anisimov, Anton Pershin, Adam Gali
abstract: Quantum relaxometry is one of the most successful applications of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond and, more broadly, solid-state spin qubits, enabling ultrasensitive detection of magnetic noise and paramagnetic species via measurements of the spin-lattice relaxation time $T_1$. Conventional pulsed protocols, however, probe $T_1$ efficiently only over a limited temporal range, which restricts the scope and throughput of the technique. Here we introduce a continuous-wave quantum relaxometry protocol that operates in the frequency domain. By measuring the frequency response of the optically detected magnetic resonance signal under low-frequency microwave amplitude modulation, we extract $T_1$ from the characteristic response time of the spin system. The method enables efficient $T_1$ measurements spanning more than three orders of magnitude -- directly demonstrated from 60 $μ$s to 200 ms in our experiments -- across a broad temperature range and under substantial ensemble inhomogeneity. We further show that this protocol enables quantitative relaxometry-based sensing in nanodiamonds, achieving a substantial speed-up over the pulsed methods and offering a practical approach to optimizing nanodiamond size for enhanced sensitivity.
summary: The authors introduce a novel continuous-wave (CW) technique to measure the spin-lattice relaxation time ($T_1$) of $	ext{NV}^-$ centers in diamond. By analyzing the frequency response of the ODMR signal, they overcome the temporal limitations of traditional pulsed methods. This CW approach allows for highly efficient and quantitative $T_1$ measurements across a wide range of timescales, making it ideal for nanoscale quantum sensing applications.
main_problem: Conventional pulsed quantum relaxometry protocols for measuring spin-lattice relaxation time (T1) are limited in temporal range and technically challenging for nanoscale systems.
main_result: A continuous-wave (CW) frequency domain protocol was introduced that efficiently measures T1 over a vast dynamic range (60 $\mu$s to 200 ms), proving superior to pulsed methods, especially for nanodiamonds.
method: The technique uses optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) with low-frequency microwave amplitude modulation and lock-in detection to extract the effective time constant ($T_{	ext{eff}}$) in the frequency domain.
model_or_system: The system utilizes Nitrogen-Vacancy ($	ext{NV}^-$) centers in diamond as solid-state spin qubits. The dynamics are modeled using Bloch equations, relating the measured frequency response to the intrinsic relaxation time $T_1$.
key_observables: Complex frequency response ($X$ and $Y$ components), effective time constant ($T_{	ext{eff}}$), and the intrinsic spin-lattice relaxation time ($T_1$).
important_parameters: Microwave power ($P_{	ext{MW}}$), laser intensity ($I$), temperature, and modulation frequency ($f_m$).
main_assumptions: The response is approximated by a first-order low-pass filter in the low-frequency limit; linearity assumptions are made when extrapolating to zero drive power.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the ODMR spectrum, the lock-in detection procedure using modulation frequency sweeps ($f_m$), and plots showing $T_{	ext{eff}}$ dependence on microwave/laser powers used to extract $T_1$.
paper_structure: The paper contrasts the limitations of time-domain pulsed protocols with the proposed continuous-wave, frequency-domain approach. It details the mathematical derivation linking the measured response function to $T_1$ and validates this method by comparing results across different diamond samples (bulk vs. nanodiamonds) under varying conditions.
why_interesting: This work provides a robust, non-invasive spectroscopic tool for characterizing spin relaxation in solid-state quantum memories, which is crucial for developing practical quantum sensors and computing elements based on NV centers.
